# Diagnosing Brake Bleeding Issues on GM V6 Platforms

When a brake pedal sinks to the floor immediately after replacing lines from the master cylinder backward, it indicates an air leak in the hydraulic system or a compromised seal within the new components themselves. On a 1998 GMC Jimmy with the 4.3L V6 engine, this specific symptom—where the vehicle eventually stops due to friction but lacks immediate stopping power—is a classic sign of low fluid volume combined with trapped air pockets that prevent pressure buildup.

The core issue here is likely not just the lines being replaced, but how the system was purged afterward. Hydraulic systems are non-compressible fluids, but air inside them is highly compressible. If the bleeding process was interrupted or if the bleeder valves were not kept fully open during the entire purge cycle, air remains in the calipers and wheel cylinders. The result is a "spongy" pedal that travels all the way to the floor before any resistance builds up.

A common mistake during this procedure involves the sequence of bleeding. While many mechanics suggest starting with the wheel furthest from the master cylinder (typically the rear driver-side on a 4-wheel disc or drum setup depending on specific configuration), skipping steps can trap air in high points of the system. If the lines were disconnected while the master cylinder reservoir was low, air will be sucked directly into the pump body, creating a cavitation effect that is extremely difficult to remove through standard bleeding.

Before assuming the master cylinder itself has failed—which would require removing the entire unit from the firewall and is indeed a time-consuming job—verify the condition of the new lines and fittings. Rubber hoses can sometimes have internal delamination where the inner liner separates, creating a micro-leak that allows fluid to bypass under pressure. Metal lines are less prone to this but can have damaged crimp points or cross-threaded banjo bolts if not torqued correctly. A loose fitting will vent brake fluid into the vacuum line of the master cylinder rather than out through the bleeder valve, causing the system to lose fluid faster than it can be replenished during bleeding.

To resolve this without replacing the master cylinder, perform a pressure bleed using a dedicated tool connected to the reservoir port. This method forces air and bubbles out through the bleeder valves more effectively than gravity bleeding. Ensure that every bleeder valve is opened fully for at least 10 seconds before closing it again; rapid opening and closing can trap bubbles in the line crevices. Check the master cylinder reservoir cap vent tube to ensure it isn't clogged, as a blocked vent creates a vacuum lock preventing fluid flow into the system during pedal application.

If the lines were replaced incorrectly or if there is an internal leak within the new assembly that cannot be sealed by simply tightening fittings, then replacing the master cylinder becomes necessary. However, given the symptoms described, a meticulous re-bleeding process combined with checking for external leaks at all connection points often resolves the issue without needing to tackle the difficult job of swapping the pump itself.
